messages.body_plain:
[Apologies for cross-posting]

I hope everyone's summers are going well.

I'm looking for a long-term (1-2 year) part-time collaborator to work on a geospatial & sociodemographic analysis of utility-scale renewable energy facilities, particularly their implications for environmental justice communities. In particular, I'm looking for someone with data science & geospatial analysis skills who can write code that can get 29 state-level, and 2 national scale energy utility data sets (up to 10,000 entries each) to speak to each other, and then conduct geospatial analysis using US census information. I have 24 of these data sets already in hand and am in the process of compiling the remaining sets. The project is not yet funded, but if this sounds like something you'd be excited to work on - let's talk!

Best,
Ingrid

--

messages.body_plain:
Many SQL databases will do this type of computation very well. One way to do it in R is to use Reduce with merge.

d1 = data.frame(key = 1:2, col1 = 3:4)
d2 = data.frame(key = 1:3, col2 = 5:7)
d3 = data.frame(key = 0:4, col3 = 8:12)
list_of_dfs = list(d1, d2, d3)
Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = "key", all = TRUE), list_of_dfs)

Produces:
  key col1 col2 col3
1   0   NA   NA    8
2   1    3    5    9
3   2    4    6   10
4   3   NA    7   11
5   4   NA   NA   12

Best,
Clark

# using dplyr

joined_df <- left_join(a, b, by=c("name")) %>%

> filter(name!="NA", name!="") %>%
> select(-starts_with("id"))

# Clean values are, at least as, if not more important, than tidy data structures.
# + Use NAs rather than "NA".  The former is a missing value; latter is a string with the letters NA, e.g., abbreviation for Nebraska.
# + z and Z appear to be considered the same in the original data and solution. So we'll make them the same, but that is a data issue.
# + Better off with name not being a factor (default in data.frame()) since it is possible that you have different levels across the 3 data frames and you need to be matching   the text.
# These are matters you should control as originator of the three data sources.

# Given the inputs......
# ######## Computational Reasoning
# A simple approach given the intended result is to use regular named subsetting.
# 1. Clean the data values
#     + Get rid of the NA and "" entries
# 2. Then use the value of the name column as rownames() for the first data.frame.
# 3. For data frames b and c, take their si and mr columns and assign using their corresponding value of name

# 1) + 2). Tidy the data values first.  Lower case to deal with z and Z. Remove rows with name being "NA" and "".
tmp2 = lapply(list(a, b, c), function(x) {
    x$name = tolower(as.character(x$name))
    w = x$name %in% c("na", "")
    x = x[!w,]
    rownames(x) = x$name
    x
})

ans = tmp2[[1]]
ans[ tmp2[[2]]$name, "si"] = tmp2[[2]]$si
ans[ tmp2[[3]]$name, "mr"] = tmp2[[3]]$mr

I can encourage enough to look at all the intermediate results, e.g.,
rownames(tmp2[[1]])
i = match(tmp2[[2]]$name, ans$name)
tmp2[[2]]$name

These truly help to understand the computations.

######### Alternative but equivalent approach, starting after computing tmp2 above - the cleaning process.
######### If you don't want named subsetting, then
ans = tmp2[[1]]

# For each name value in tmp2[[2]], what is the corresponding index in ans$name
# These are the rows we want.
i = match(tmp2[[2]]$name, ans$name)
ans[ i, "si"] = tmp2[[2]]$si

i = match(tmp2[[3]]$name, ans$name)
ans[ i, "mr"] = tmp2[[2]]$mr

messages.body_plain:
Hi D-RUG,

I'm trying to make a lovely UpSetR plot with 17 sets. Is anyone familiar with these? I know that there are overlaps between all 17 sets. However, my plots do not reflect this. Below is some code with a downloadable set of data.

# Download and import to a data.frame
if(!file.exists('presence_absence.csv')){download.file('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/johnsolk/RNAseq_15killifish/master/evaluation/presence_absence.csv', 'presence_absence.csv')}
pa <- read.csv("presence_absence.csv")
pa <- pa[,-c(1)]
rownames(pa) <- pa$Ensembl
pa <- pa[,-c(1)]

# This plot will display 4 intersects
upset(pa, sets = c(c("A_xenica","F_catanatus"),c("F_chrysotus","F_diaphanus")),mb.ratio = c(0.55, 0.45),keep.order = F)

# As soon as I move to 6, I am confused - there is no longer a bar crossing all 6 sets
upset(pa, sets = c(c("A_xenica","F_catanatus","F_notatus"), c("F_chrysotus","F_diaphanus","F_nottii")),mb.ratio = c(0.55, 0.45),nsets = 6,keep.order = F)

# The full 17 sets does not make any sense
upset(pa, sets = c(c("A_xenica","F_catanatus"),c("F_chrysotus","F_diaphanus"),c("F_grandis","F_heteroclitusMDPL"),c("F_heteroclitusMDPP","F_notatus"),c("F_nottii","F_olivaceous"),c("F_parvapinis","F_rathbuni"),c("F_sciadicus","F_similis"),c("F_zebrinus","L_goodei"),c("L_parva")),mb.ratio = c(0.55, 0.45),keep.order = F)

# Confirming that there are overlaps between all 17 sets (and 16, 15, 14, etc)
test<- rowSums(pa)
test<- as.data.frame(test)
colnames(test) <- c("sum")
sum(test$sum == 17)
sum(test$sum == 16)
sum(test$sum == 15)
sum(test$sum == 14)

Any insight anyone has would be greatly appreciated.

Much thanks!

Cheers,
Lisa

--
Lisa K. Johnson
Ph.D. Candidate
Lab for Data Intensive Biology
University of California, Davis
